name: Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome (GTPS)
summary: Lateral hip pain commonly associated with gluteal tendon pathology and compression sensitivity around the greater trochanter; isolated bursitis is an oversimplification.

looksLike: Pain with stairs, single-leg stance or prolonged walking
redFlags: Inability to weight bear after trauma
Cancer history, unexplained weight loss or severe night pain
firstSteps: Reduce sustained hip adduction/compressive positions; modify side-lying with pillow support

assess: Single-leg loading may reproduce familiar pain

tests.name: 30-Second Single-Leg Stance Test
tests.purpose: Assess lateral hip pain provocation during single-leg loading.
tests.positive: Familiar lateral hip pain reproduced within 30 seconds.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Reduce sustained hip adduction/compressive positions; modify side-lying with pillow support
dose: Hip abduction isometric: 4–5 x 20–30 seconds, tolerable effort
Avoid prolonged painful side-lying on affected side
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress gluteal tendon loading and hip abductor strength
Build pelvic control in functional single-leg tasks
Gradually restore stairs and longer walks
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Progress running, hills, lateral movement and work demands
Increase single-leg load and speed gradually
dose: Walk/run volume progressed gradually; avoid simultaneous large increases in speed and distance
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Hip abductor strength appropriate for target activity

structures: Greater trochanteric bursa and iliotibial band interface
mechanism: Repeated tendon compression in hip adduction
Abrupt increase in walking, running or side-lying pressure
Reduced hip abductor capacity may contribute
classification: Coexisting hip OA or lumbar referral
investigations: Usually clinical; ultrasound/MRI for uncertain diagnosis, suspected tendon tear or persistent symptoms.
Urgent imaging/referral if stress fracture or acute fracture suspected.
manual: Manual therapy may address coexisting hip or lumbar mobility limitation but is not a primary tendon treatment.
Avoid aggressive direct compression over greater trochanter in irritable cases.
modalities: Pillow positioning and load modification may reduce compression.
Passive modalities do not replace progressive tendon loading.
mistakes: Calling all lateral hip pain bursitis
Ignoring lumbar and hip OA differential
pearls: Education about compression plus progressive loading is central.
Pain on palpation alone is insufficient to identify a specific tendon lesion.

tests.name: 30-Second Single-Leg Stance Test
tests.purpose: Assess lateral hip pain provocation during single-leg loading.
tests.positive: Familiar lateral hip pain reproduced within 30 seconds.
tests.patientPosition: Stand near support; patient stands on symptomatic leg for up to 30 seconds while pelvis and trunk are observed.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports GTPS when combined with history and other tests; not a stand-alone diagnosis.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
